The
 effects
 of

 on
 the
 biotransformation
 of
 the

 dye
Direct  Black
 22
 (DB22)
 and
 of
 its
 anaerobic
 by-products
 (aromatic
 amines)
 were
 tested
 using
sequencing
 batch
 reactors.
 The
 experimental
 set-up
 consisted
 of
 three
 independent
 reactors
(R1,
 R2,
 and
 R3)
 working
 with
 distinct
 cycles:
 R1
 was
 completely
 anaerobic,
 while
 both
 R2
and
 R3
 included
 a
 micro-aerated
 stage
 after
 an
 anaerobic
 stage
 (R2
 continuously
 and
 R3
intermittently
 micro-aerated).
 Average
 DB22
 removal
 efﬁciencies
 in
 R1,
 R2,
 and
 R3
 were
81.4,
 74.5
 and
 76.8%,
 respectively.
 R1
 produced
 an
 efﬂuent
 with
 high
 acute
 ecotoxicity
 (1.13%
as
 effective
 concentration
 causing
 50%
 of
 bioluminescence
 inhibition
 in
 Vibrio
 ﬁscheri)
 due
to
 aromatic
 amines
 accumulation.
 In
 contrast,
 no
 acute
 ecotoxicity
 was
 detected
 in
 the
efﬂuent
 of
 R2
 and
 R3,
 reﬂecting
 aromatic
 amines
 removal.
 At
 the
 anaerobic
 stage
 of
 the
cycle,
 R2
 and
 R3
 showed
 DB22
 decolorization
 rates
 73
 and
 123%
 higher
 than
 R1,
 respectively.
At
 the
 same
 time,
 the
 corresponding
 values
 of
 estimated
 methane
 production
 were
 35
 and
37%
 lower.
 Thus,
 oxygen
 apparently
 changed
 the
 balance
 between
 methanogenesis
 and
reductive
 decolorization,
 inhibiting
 the
 ﬁrst
 process
 and
 enhancing
 the
 second.

1.
 
Introduction
In
 textile
 industry,
 dye
 ﬁxation
 to fabrics
 occurs
 only
 partially
 (50–98%),
generating
 wastewater
 with
 high
 coloration.
 The
 main
 pigments
 used
in
 this
 sector
 are
 azo
 dyes
 (about
 70%),
 which
 are
 featured
 by
 the
presence
 of azo
 bonds
 ( 
N
 
N 
).
 The
 azo
 dyes
 and
 their
 anaerobic
degradation
 by-products
 can
 be
 mutagenic,
 carcinogenic,
 and
 toxic
 to
the
 environment.
 High
 coloration
 may
 also
 inhibit
 photosynthesis
 in
water
 bodies
 (van
 der
 Zee
 and
 Villaverde,
 2005; dos
 Santos
 et
 al.,
 2007).
To
 solve
 this
 problem,
 biological
 treatment
 stands
 out
 as
 a low-cost
environmental-friendly
 alternative
 that
 can
 be
 used
 in
 industries
 of
diverse
 scales.
 Generally,
 biological
 treatment
 removes
 azo
 dyes
 and
their
 by-products
 from
 textile
 wastewater
 by
 a combination
 of
 anaer-

 authors.

obic
 and
 aerobic
 processes
 (Field
 et
 al.,
 1995). An
 initial
 anaerobic
 step
is
 required
 since
 azo
 dyes
 are
 known
 to
 generally
 remain
 unaffected
under
 aerobic
 conditions
 (Pagga
 and
 Brown,
 1986; Shaul
 et
 al.,
 1991).
The
 azo
 bonds
 are
 highly
 electrophilic,
 which
 protects
 the
 dye
 molecule
against
 attacks
 by
 oxygenase
 enzymes
 (Kulla
 et
 al.,
 1983; Field
 et
 al.,
1995).
On
 the
 other
 hand,
 the
 anaerobic
 cleavage
 of
 azo
 bonds,
 the
 chro-
mophore
 groups,
 reduces
 the
 efﬂuent
 coloration
 through
 the
 action
of
 non-speciﬁc
 exoenzymes
 (azoreductases).
 The
 dye
 acts
 as
 an
 elec-
tron
 acceptor
 during
 the
 degradation
 of
 an
 organic
 substrate.
 Aromatic
amines
 are
 formed
 after
 the
 reduction
 of
 azo
 bonds.
 Such
 compounds
are
 colorless,
 although
 they
 can
 be
 highly
 toxic.
 These
 amines
 are
 then
degraded
 aerobically,
 acting
 as
 energy
 and
 carbon
 source
 (van
 der
 Zee
and
 Villaverde,
 2005; Khan
 et
 al.,
 2013; Arora,
 2015).

Due
 to
 what
 has
 been
 mentioned,
 the
 use
 of
 two
 treatment
 units
(anaerobic
 followed
 by
 aerobic)
 is
 frequent
 (Jonstrup
 et
 al.,
 2011; da
Silva
 et
 al.,
 2012; Amaral
 et
 al.,
 2014; Baêta
 et
 al.,
 2015). Neverthe-
less,
 anaerobic
 and
 aerobic
 mixed
 microbial
 cultures
 may
 be
 able
 to
reduce
 azo
 bonds
 and
 degrade
 aromatic
 amines
 when
 in
 the
 absence
and
 presence
 of
 oxygen,
 respectively
 (Field
 et
 al.,
 1995). This
 suggests
the
 development
 of
 a compact
 treatment
 in
 a single
 unit
 subject
 to
 the
two
 conditions
 (anaerobic
 and
 aerobic)
 over
 time.
 It
 was
 also
 observed
that
 micro-aeration,
 under
 5–10%
 of
 the
 oxygen
 saturation
 concentra-
tion,
 may
 be
 enough
 to mineralize
 most
 of
 the
 biodegradable
 aromatic
compounds
 (Field
 et al.,
 1995; Gavazza
 et
 al.,
 2015; Kumar
 et
 al.,
 2015).
In
 a practical
 approach,
 sequencing
 batch
 reactors
 (SBR)
 are
 an
appropriate
 alternative
 for
 the
 treatment
 of
 intermittently
 produced
wastewater.
 This
 is
 due
 to
 the
 hydraulic
 regime
 of
 these
 reactors,
 which
do
 not
 work
 with
 a continuous
 feed,
 by
 their
 very
 deﬁnition.
 Addition-
ally,
 reactors
 without
 continuous
 discharge
 may
 accumulate
 oxygen
in
 the
 aerated
 phases,
 causing
 unnecessary
 electric
 energy
 consump-
tion
 in
 treatment
 units.
 Intermittent
 aeration
 can
 be
 an
 alternative
 to
keep
 low
 concentrations
 of
 oxygen
 in
 this
 case.
 However,
 few
 stud-
ies
 have
 been
 published
 regarding
 the
 combination
 of
 anaerobic
 and
micro-aerobic
 conditions
 for
 azo
 dye
 degradation
 in
 the
 same
 com-
partment
 (Gavazza
 et
 al.,
 2015; Balapure
 et
 al.,
 2016). Even
 fewer
 tested
the
 use
 of
 intermittent
 micro-aeration
 (Kumar
 et
 al.,
 2015).
With
 this
 background,
 this
 study
 aimed
 to
 evaluate
 the
 effects
of
 continuous
 and
 intermittent
 micro-aeration,
 both
 applied
 after
 an
anaerobic
 step,
 on
 tetra-azo
 dye
 Direct
 Black
 22
 (DB22)
 and
 its
 by-
products
 transformation,
 using
 biological
 sequencing
 batch
 reactors.
2.
 
Materials
 and
 methods
2.1.
 
Synthetic
 wastewater
Tetra-azo
 dye
 Direct
 Black
 22
 (DB22;
 C44H32N13Na3O11S3;
molecular
 weight:
 1083.97
 g
 mol−1; CAS
 #
 6473-13-8)
 was
obtained
 from
 ExataCor©. Dye
 purity
 was not
 provided,
 thus
nuclear
 magnetic
 resonance
 (NMR)
 spectroscopy
 was
 applied
for
 its
 determination
 before
 starting
 the
 experiment,
 as
described
 in
 the
 Supplementary
 material.
 DB22
 purity
 was
found
 to
 be
 50%
 on
 a
 mass
 basis.
Synthetic
 efﬂuent
 was designed
 to
 reproduce
 real
 tex-
tile
 
wastewater,
 
following
 
recommendation
 
of
 
Amorim
et
 al.
 (2013). It
 was composed
 of:
 DB22
 (0.03
 mM),
 ethanol
(1200
 mg L−1 of
 Chemical
 Oxygen
 Demand
 —
 COD),
 NaHCO3
as
 buffer
 (1200
 mg  L−1),
 NaCl
 as
 a
 usual
 interfering
 substance
in
 textile
 efﬂuents
 (1000
 mg  L−1),
 macro
 and
 micronutrients.
DB22
 dissolution
 in
 water
 followed
 the
 procedures
 of
 Gavazza
et
 al.
 (2015). Ethanol
 is
 not
 a
 common
 component
 of
 real
 textile
wastewaters.
 Starch
 is
 more
 common.
 However,
 for
 practical
reasons,
 ethanol
 was chosen
 as
 electron
 donor
 for
 the
 azo
 dye
reduction
 in
 the
 present
 work.
The
 macronutrients
 concentrations
 in
 the
 synthetic
 efﬂu-
ent
 were
 (mg
 L−1):
 NH4Cl
 (280),
 K2HPO4 (252),
 MgSO4·7H2O
(100)
 and
 CaCl2 (7),
 adapted
 from
 dos
 Santos
 et
 al.
 (2006d).
The
 amount
 of
 1
 mL  L−1 of
 micronutrients
 solution
 (Florêncio
et
 al.,
 1993)
 was added
 to
 the
 synthetic
 efﬂuent
 and
 it
 was
composed
 of
 (mg
 L−1):
 FeCl2·4H2O
 (2000),
 H3BO3 (50),
 ZnCl2
(50),
 MnCl2·4H2O
 (500),

 (38),

 Resazurin
was

 of
 its
 properties

 a
 redox
 mediator
(dos
 Santos
 et
 al.,
 2006).
2.2.
 
Experimental
 set-up
The
 experimental
 set-up
 consisted
 of
 three
 independent
sequencing
 batch
 reactors
 (R1,
 R2,
 and
 R3)
 working
 with
distinct
 anaerobic/micro-aerobic
 cycle
 operating
 conditions.
Cylindrical
 acrylic
 reactors
 (20
 cm
 of
 internal
 diameter
 and
19
 cm
 of
 height)
 with
 5
 L of
 working
 volume
 (replacement
volume
 of
 50%)
 were
 operated
 at
 mesophilic
 temperature
 of
37
 ±
 1 ◦C
 for
 107
 days.
In
 each
 reactor,
 the
 cycle
 time
 was
 24
 h
 distributed
between:
 ﬁlling
 (15
 min),
 reacting
 (23
 h),
 settling
 (30
 min),
 and
drawling
 (15
 min).
 The
 23
 h
 of
 reaction
 time
 in
 R1
 was
 com-
pletely
 anaerobic.
 R2
 combined
 12
 h
 of
 anaerobic
 stage
 and
11
 h
 of
 micro-aerated
 stage
 in
 the
 reaction
 time.
 R3
 operated
similarly
 to
 R2,
 with
 intermittent
 air
 supply
 (30
 min
 every
 2
 h)
in
 the
 11
 h
 of
 the
 micro-aerated
 stage.
Circular
 aerators
 made
 of
 micro-perforated
 rubber
 (Resun,
Air
 Curtain,
 Raoping,
 China),
 placed
 at
 the
 bottom
 of
 R2
 and
R3,
 were
 responsible
 for
 sparging
 the
 air
 at
 a
 ﬂow
 rate
 of
0.25
 ±
 0.05
 L
 min−1 (measured
 with
 a
 Tecnoﬂuid
 ﬂowmeter,
TRV-140-K-7-P,
 Nova
 Lima,
 Brazil)
 producing
 few
 ﬁne
 bubbles.
Timers
 (Clip,
 CLB-40,
 São
 Roque,
 Brazil)
 were
 used
 to
 control
the
 power
 supply
 for
 the
 aerator
 (Jad,
 Air-Pump
 S-2000,
 Raop-
ing,
 China)
 in
 R2
 and
 R3.
Anaerobic
 sludge
 from
 a
 pilot
 scale
 UASB
 reactor
 treat-
ing
 real
 textile
 wastewater,
 previously
 operated
 by
 Amaral
et
 al.
 (2014), was used
 as
 inoculum
 (2.5
 gVSS
 L−1 in
 the
 mixed
liquor).
 Substrate-biomass
 contact
 was
 ensured
 by
 magnetic
stirrers
 (Quimis,
 Q-241,
 Diadema,
 Brazil),
 during
 the
 reaction
phase.
2.3.
 
Analytical
 procedure
Samples
 taken
 from
 the
 outlet
 of
 the
 reactors
 at
 the
 end
 of
the
 cycle
 time
 were
 analyzed
 three
 times

 week
 by
 measuring
pH,
 alkalinity,
 oxidation-reduction
 potential
 (ORP),
 dissolved
oxygen
 (DO),
 salinity,
 COD,
 DB22
 concentration,
 and
 aromatic
amines
 (qualitatively).
 Volatile
 suspended
 solids
 (VSS)
 in
 the
efﬂuent
 were
 monitored
 fortnightly.
 VSS
 were
 also
 measured
in
 the
 mixed
 liquor
 on
 the
 ﬁrst
 and
 on
 the
 last
 operational
days.
Temporal
 concentration
 proﬁles
 were
 performed
 after
 the
reactors
 reached
 apparent
 steady-state
 conditions.
 The
 mea-
sured
 parameters
 were:
 ORP,

 fatty
 acids
(VFA),
 DB22
 concentration,
 and
 aromatic
 amines
 (qualita-
tively)
 over
 the

 of
 24
 h.
DB22
 and
 aromatic

 were
 monitored

tometrically
 (Hitachi
 U-2910,

 Ltd.,
 Tokyo,
 Japan).
Samples

 15
 min
 at
 3500
 rpm
 and
 the
 clar-
iﬁed

 diluted
 to

 absorbance
to
 values
 lower
 than
 0.9

 wavelengths
 of
 interest.
DB22
 maximum
 wavelength
 of

 absorption
 is
 476
 nm,
which
 was
 used
 for
 measuring
 its
 concentration.
 The
 molar
absorption
 coefﬁcient,
 i.e.

 factor
 to
 convert
 absorbance
 mea-
surements
 into
 concentration,
 was 56.2
 cm−1 mM−1.
Qualitative
 analysis
 of
 aromatic
 amines
 was performed
 by
scanning
 the
 samples
 in
 the
 light
 absorption
 range
 of

compounds
 (200–350
 nm)
 (Pinheiro
 et
 al.,
 2004).
 This
 method
is
 commonly
 used

Amaral
